title: Types of Genetic Tests and Their Clinical Applications
summary: Diagnostic, predictive, carrier, pharmacogenomic, and prenatal tests — matching the right test to the clinical question.

content_blocks.text: Matching the Test to the Clinical Question

Genetic testing is not monolithic. Ordering 'a genetic test' without specifying the clinical question is like ordering 'an imaging study.' Each test type has a specific indication, sensitivity, and result interpretation framework. The appropriate test depends on whether you're confirming a diagnosis, predicting future risk, identifying carriers, or guiding drug therapy.

concepts.definition: Confirms or rules out a genetic condition in someone with symptoms — e.g., whole-exome sequencing for a child with developmental delay
Identifies disease risk before symptoms — e.g., BRCA1/2 testing in a woman with family history of breast cancer
Determines if an asymptomatic person carries one copy of a recessive variant — e.g., CF carrier screening before pregnancy
Predicts drug response based on metabolizer phenotype — e.g., CYP2D6 for codeine, DPYD for fluorouracil
Screens or diagnoses fetal chromosomal/genetic conditions — includes NIPT, amniocentesis, CVS
Population-level dried blood spot testing for ~35 core conditions by RUSP — enables pre-symptomatic treatment

content_blocks.text: Karyotyping examines chromosome number and large structural rearrangements visible under a microscope — appropriate for Down syndrome (trisomy 21) or chromosomal translocations. Chromosomal microarray (CMA) adds resolution for submicroscopic copy-number variants (CNVs). Sequence-based tests (panels, WES, WGS) detect single-nucleotide variants and small indels. RNA sequencing (transcriptomics) and methylation arrays add expression-level data.

content_blocks.label: Conditions on the federal RUSP newborn screening panel
content_blocks.context: States may screen for additional conditions; all 50 states screen for at least the 35 RUSP core conditions using dried blood spots from heel-stick sampling

content_blocks.body: DTC services (e.g., 23andMe, AncestryDNA) use genotyping arrays that test only known variants and cannot detect rare pathogenic variants. A 'negative' BRCA result from a DTC test does NOT rule out hereditary breast/ovarian cancer risk. Patients presenting DTC results should be referred to genetic counselors for appropriate clinical-grade testing.
content_blocks.title: Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) Genomics: Clinical Limitations

content_blocks.text: Genetic counselors play an indispensable role in pre-test education (informed consent, implications for family members) and post-test interpretation. The NSGC (National Society of Genetic Counselors) and ABGC (American Board of Genetic Counseling) credential these specialists. Many states now mandate genetic counselor involvement for high-complexity results.
